newsitem.title: USA: US Treasuries close higher on April PPI drop.
newsitem.headline: US Treasuries close higher on April PPI drop.

text.p: U.S. Treasury prices ended higher on Wednesday after the government reported that U.S. wholesale prices dropped in April.

The Labor Department's Producer Price Index (PPI) fell 0.6 percent in April. The core PPI, which excludes the food and energy components, slipped 0.1 percent. A 0.1 percent increase had been forecast for the core rate.
"The PPI news was the main factor pushing bond prices higher," said Michael Moran, chief economist at Daiwa Securities America, a primary government securities dealer.
The benchmark 30-year Treasury bond price rose above 97 and its yield fell to around 6.85 percent in the aftermath of the favorable wholesale price reoprt.

By midday, however, profit-taking nibbled at the advance. At mid-afternoon, an unconfirmed rumor that a Washington-based newsletter had said that Treasury Secretary Rubin would be comfortable with a slightly weaker dollar -- 115 yen was mentioned -- encouraged dollar sales. The U.S. unit weakened and U.S. Treasury securities prices cut about a third of their gains before staging a partial recovery.
The 30-year bond ended at 96-21/32, yielding 6.89 percent.
Charles Lieberman, chief economist at Chase Securities Inc., said there were several reasons why the bond market did not stage an all-out rally on the wholesale price news.

One was that while the PPI was "very friendly" for the bond market, it reflected "the same outstanding news on inflation that we've been seeing" but could not assure the market that current, tight labor market conditions would not generate inflation pressures in the future, he said.
Another reason for the lack of an exuberant rally was the weakness in the dollar, Lieberman said.
"The dollar actually traded below 117 yen," he said.

"A weaker dollar suggests that foreign investors perhaps will be a little more fearful about buying dollar denominated assets. It could reflect less confidence that the Federal Reserve will tighten monetary policy," said Lieberman.
"The weaker dollar definitely curbed some of the appetite for U.S. Treasuries," said Kevin Flanagan, first vice president and money market economist at Dean Witter Reynolds.
Moran said another reason that the market could not hold its best gains on Wednesday is that the April Consumer Price Index (CPI) is due on Thursday.
